units.text: The June 2022 HTTP standard (RFC 9110, RFC 9111, RFC 9112) is the worldwide standard, and RFC 9112 confirms the authority-form of request-target applies only to CONNECT requests. No evidence in the supplied sources states that a DELETE request establishes a tunnel per this standard.

citations.title: HTTP/1.1 Explained: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 Messages, Methods and Security | Safeguard Blog

judgement.reason: The passages identify RFC 9110/9111/9112 as the June 2022 HTTP standards, RFC 9112 states the authority-form is only used for CONNECT requests, and no passage says a DELETE request establishes a tunnel.

units.text: CONNECT method (RFC 7231 §4.3.6) is the HTTP method that requests establishing a tunnel, as documented in the same RFC lineage. DELETE is a state-changing method unrelated to tunnel establishment.

judgement.reason: The passages support that CONNECT requests establishing a tunnel, but they do not mention RFC 7231 §4.3.6 or DELETE being a state-changing method unrelated to tunnel establishment.

units.text: Tunnel behavior is defined as a blind relay between connections (RFC 9110 §3.7), but no cited source associates initiating a tunnel with a DELETE request under the June 2022 HTTP standard.

citations.title: HTTP/1.1 Explained: RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 Messages, Methods and Security | Safeguard Blog

judgement.reason: The RFC 9110 passage defines a tunnel as a blind relay between two connections and only says a tunnel might be initiated by an HTTP request, while the other passage attributes tunnel initiation to CONNECT; no cited passage associates it with DELETE.

labelled_source_agreement.reason: Both the reference and the system account identify CONNECT, not DELETE, as the method that establishes a tunnel.
